Oxygen therapy: Crucial for hypoxemic patients to reduce pulmonary vasoconstriction and improve oxygen delivery.

qs.q: What is the primary target for oxygen therapy in a patient with pneumonia who presents with hypoxaemia?
qs.e: Oxygen is indicated to maintain the PaO2 at 8 kPa (60 mmHg) or greater, or SaO2 < 92% targets. Over-oxygenating patients with chronic obstructive hypercapnia can lead to complications, but the general target focuses on preventing severe hypoxia.

qs.q: What is the minimum recommended duration per day for long-term domiciliary oxygen therapy (LTOT) to provide significant benefit in specific patients with COPD?
o: A minimum duration of 15 hours per day
Continuous 24 hours without any short breaks
Only during brief periods of acute physical exercise
Precisely 4 hours restricted only during sleep
qs.e: Long-term domiciliary oxygen therapy provides significant benefit when used for a minimum of 15 hours per day, with greater benefits seen in those receiving over 20 hours per day.

qs.q: Why must high-concentration oxygen therapy be avoided or carefully controlled in patients with chronic respiratory failure?
o: It causes immediate, irreversible pulmonary oxygen toxicity and alveolar fibrosis
It removes their hypoxemic respiratory drive, slowing breathing and leading to CO2 retention, falling pH, and coma
It rapidly precipitates severe systemic hypertension and left ventricular failure
It completely neutralizes the bronchodilating effects of concurrently administered anticholinergics
qs.e: These patients depend on hypoxemia for their respiratory drive. High oxygen concentrations slow down breathing, causing carbon dioxide to rise, pH to drop, and potentially sending the patient into a coma.

es.q: A critically ill patient develops acute respiratory failure refractory to oxygen therapy, with bilateral pulmonary infiltrates on chest X-ray, in the absence of primary cardiac failure. Describe the hallmark microscopic finding characteristic of the acute phase of this condition (ARDS), and briefly
es.m: The hallmark microscopic finding characteristic of the acute phase of ARDS (Diffuse Alveolar Damage) is the presence of **hyaline membranes** lining the alveolar ducts and alveoli (2 marks). The initial cellular events in its pathogenesis involve an insult that triggers pulmonary macrophages to release **IL-8** (1 mark), leading to neutrophil chemotaxis into the alveolar space (1 mark). These activated neutrophils then release damaging oxidants and proteases (1 mark).

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Oxygen therapy corrects hypoxaemia, improves tissue oxygen delivery and reduces pulmonary vasoconstriction. In low‑resource hospitals clinicians must decide when to start, how much, and monitor for CO₂ retention and fire risk.

sections.p: Oxygen therapy is the delivery of a higher fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO₂) than ambient air to treat hypoxaemia (low arterial oxygen). Diagnosis relies on pulse oximetry (SpO₂) or arterial blood gas (PaO₂).
b: SpO₂ < 90 % (or < 88 % in COPD) indicates need for supplemental O₂.
PaO₂ < 55 mmHg (7.3 kPa) is the threshold for long‑term therapy.

sections.p: Severity is graded by PaO₂ or SpO₂ and clinical impact (dyspnoea, organ dysfunction).
b: Mild: SpO₂ 90‑94 % (no organ dysfunction).
Moderate: SpO₂ 88‑89 % or PaO₂ 55‑60 mmHg, dyspnoea on exertion.
Severe: SpO₂ < 88 % or PaO₂ < 55 mmHg, signs of right‑heart strain or polycythaemia.

sections.p: Identify the underlying cause of hypoxaemia; common in East Africa include:
b: Pneumonia (bacterial, TB, malaria‑related pulmonary oedema).
Acute severe asthma or COPD exacerbation (often with biomass smoke exposure).
Pulmonary embolism (post‑surgery, HIV‑associated hypercoagulability).
Severe anaemia (sickle cell crisis, malaria).
High‑altitude exposure (rural highland clinics).

sections.p: Patients appear cyanotic, tachypnoeic, with altered mental status if severe. In COPD, they may retain CO₂ and have a “quiet” chest.
b: Peripheral cyanosis, especially lips and nail beds.
Respiratory rate > 30/min, use of accessory muscles.
Confusion or lethargy when PaO₂ < 50 mmHg.

t.b: Is the patient hypoxaemic? – SpO₂ < 90 % confirms need for O₂; if unavailable, use clinical signs.
What is the exact PaO₂, PaCO₂ and pH? – PaO₂ < 55 mmHg triggers LTOT; PaCO₂ > 45 mmHg warns of CO₂ retention.
What is the underlying lung pathology? – Consolidation, pleural effusion, pneumothorax guide specific treatment.
Is polycythaemia present? – Hb > 18 g/dL supports LTOT indication.

sections.p: Complications arise from both under‑ and over‑oxygenation.
b: CO₂ retention in COPD – rising PaCO₂, decreasing pH.
Oxygen‑induced hypercapnia – worsening dyspnoea, confusion.
Fire risk – avoid oxygen near open flames or smoking.
Absorption atelectasis – prolonged high FiO₂ > 60 % without ventilation.

sections.p: Treat the cause first, then give oxygen using the simplest device available.
b: Nasal cannula 1‑4 L/min for mild‑moderate hypoxaemia (FiO₂ ≈ 0.24‑0.40).
Simple face mask 5‑10 L/min for moderate‑severe (FiO₂ ≈ 0.40‑0.60).
Non‑rebreather mask 10‑15 L/min if SpO₂ < 85 % (FiO₂ ≈ 0.80).
High‑flow nasal oxygen (if available) for severe COVID‑19 or ARDS.
Long‑term oxygen therapy (LTOT) ≥ 15 h/day for chronic PaO₂ < 55 mmHg, with smoking cessation.
Avoid humidified O₂ in COPD with CO₂ retention unless mucosal dryness is severe.

sections.p: Re‑assess oxygen needs daily; for chronic users arrange home oxygen assessment and smoking cessation counseling.
b: Repeat SpO₂ after 30 min of therapy to confirm response.
Monitor for CO₂ retention with repeat ABG if mental status changes.
Educate patients on fire safety and device maintenance.

sections.p: Conditions that mimic hypoxaemia but need different treatment.
b: Carbon monoxide poisoning – normal SpO₂, treat with 100 % O₂ and hyperbaric therapy.
Methemoglobinemia – low pulse‑ox reading, chocolate‑brown blood, treat with methylene blue.

sections.p: Certain measurements may be falsely reassuring.
b: Pulse oximetry over nail polish or dark skin can overestimate SpO₂.
ABG on room air after recent high‑flow O₂ may underestimate true hypoxia if patient is weaned too quickly.

whenToSeekHelp: Progressive dyspnoea despite O₂, new confusion, or SpO₂ < 80 % – call senior or arrange transfer to ICU.

faq.q: Why can oxygen worsen CO₂ retention in COPD?
faq.a: High FiO₂ reduces hypoxic drive and worsens V/Q mismatch, leading to CO₂ buildup.
Not in COPD; humidification can increase airway resistance and worsen CO₂ retention.
Chronic PaO₂ < 55 mmHg, or 55‑60 mmHg with cor pulmonale, polycythaemia, or pulmonary hypertension, for ≥ 15 h/day.

exam: A 55‑year‑old man with COPD presents with SpO₂ 84 % – what is the immediate oxygen target and why? — Aim for SpO₂ 88‑92 % to avoid hypercapnia while correcting hypoxia.
A child with severe malaria has SpO₂ 86 % – which device is most appropriate in a district hospital? — Simple face mask 5‑10 L/min because nasal cannula may not deliver sufficient FiO₂.

You suspect pulmonary embolism in a postpartum woman with sudden hypoxia – what investigation guides oxygen therapy? — ABG to assess PaO₂/PaCO₂; if PaO₂ < 55 mmHg start high‑flow O₂ and arrange CT‑PA if available.
A patient on LTOT continues to smoke – what is the key management step? — Immediate cessation counseling and removal of home oxygen until smoking stops, due to fire risk.

During a TB treatment course a patient develops worsening dyspnoea and SpO₂ 82 % – what differential should you consider and how does it affect oxygen use? — Consider drug‑induced pneumonitis; give O₂ while evaluating with chest X‑ray.

In a remote clinic you have only a pulse oximeter – how do you decide on oxygen flow without ABG? — Use SpO₂ thresholds: < 90 % (non‑COPD) or < 88 % (COPD) start low‑flow O₂ and reassess after 15 min.

A patient with severe asthma receives nebulised bronchodilators and O₂; after 30 min SpO₂ improves but PaCO₂ rises – what does this indicate? — Developing CO₂ retention; consider reducing FiO₂ and preparing for non‑invasive ventilation.

Explain why high‑flow nasal oxygen may be preferred over a non‑rebreather in COVID‑19 ARDS in a low‑resource ICU. — HFNO provides heated, humidified O₂ at up to 60 L/min, improves comfort and reduces work of breathing while delivering precise FiO₂.
